theme: Doctrinal Pause: The Three Offices of Christ, Prophet, Priest, King
doctrine: The Three Offices of Christ, Prophet, Priest, King
summary: Christ as the fulfillment of every OT office, prophet like Moses, priest like Melchizedek, king like David
readingInstruction: Read Deuteronomy 18:15-19, Psalm 110, and Hebrews 1:1-4. Take your time with these three short passages. They each speak of one of the three offices that God established in Israel, prophet, priest, and king, and the way that all three come together in Jesus.
settingTheScene: Today’s reading pauses in the middle of the laws of Deuteronomy, just before the chapter that sets out the roles of kings, priests, and prophets in Israel (Deuteronomy 17 and 18). It pauses to ask a question that will come up many times in the story ahead: how do the offices of Israel point to Christ? The three passages you read today are central. Moses promises a prophet like himself, David writes of a king who is also a priest forever, and the writer of Hebrews says that in Jesus, God has spoken his final word.
observation: “The LORD your God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among you, from your brothers; it is to him you shall listen” (Deuteronomy 18:15).
“I will put my words in his mouth, and he shall speak to them all that I command him” (Deuteronomy 18:18).
“The LORD says to my Lord: Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool” (Psalm 110:1).
“The LORD has sworn and will not change his mind: You are a priest forever after the order of Melchizedek” (Psalm 110:4).
“He will execute judgment among the nations, filling them with corpses” (Psalm 110:6).
“Long ago, at many times and in many ways, God spoke to our fathers by the prophets, but in these last days he has spoken to us by his Son” (Hebrews 1:1-2).
“He is the radiance of the glory of God and the exact imprint of his nature, and he upholds the universe by the word of his power” (Hebrews 1:3).
“After making purification for sins, he sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high” (Hebrews 1:3).
doctrinalFocus:
The three offices of Christ is a way of organizing what the Bible teaches about who Jesus is and what he does. It was developed by John Calvin and has been used by Reformed and many other Christian traditions ever since. It rests on a simple observation: in the Old Testament, three kinds of people were anointed to serve God’s people, the prophet, the priest, and the king. Each represents a way in which God relates to his people. Each was incomplete. And all three find their fulfillment in the one called Messiah, which means “Anointed One.”

Consider the prophet first. A prophet speaks for God to the people. Moses was the model prophet, to whom God spoke “mouth to mouth” (Numbers 12:8). In Deuteronomy 18, Moses promises that God would one day raise up another like him. Over the centuries, many prophets came, but the people kept waiting for the prophet. Jesus is that prophet, and more. The Gospel of John says, “No one has ever seen God; the only God, who is at the Father’s side, he has made him known” (John 1:18). Where prophets spoke the word of God, Jesus is the Word of God. Hebrews 1 says that God has now spoken by his Son. As prophet, Christ reveals the Father to us and teaches us the truth. He does this through his own teaching, through the Spirit who inspired the Scriptures, and through the Spirit who illumines our hearts.

Consider the priest next. A priest speaks to God on behalf of the people. He offers sacrifices, makes intercession, and blesses. The priests of Israel, from Aaron onward, did this imperfectly. They were sinners, and they died, so that new priests were always needed. Psalm 110:4 announces a priest of another kind, “after the order of Melchizedek,” a priest forever. Hebrews develops this at length. Jesus is the great high priest who has offered, once for all, the perfect sacrifice, namely himself (Hebrews 7:27). He continually intercedes for us at the right hand of God (Romans 8:34; Hebrews 7:25). As priest, Christ reconciles us to God by his death and keeps us in fellowship with him by his prayers.

Consider the king last. A king rules the people on behalf of God. David was the model king, and God promised him a son who would reign forever (2 Samuel 7). Psalm 110:1 says that David’s Lord sits at God’s right hand until his enemies are made a footstool. Jesus applied this psalm to himself (Matthew 22:41-45). He is the king who has been raised and exalted, who rules now over his church and the universe, and who will return to judge and to bring all things under his feet. As king, Christ governs us by his word and Spirit, defends us from our enemies, and will finally subdue all things.

Why do the three offices matter? Because they correct our one-sided views of Jesus. Some think of him only as a teacher, a moral guide who gave us a better way to live. That is the prophet without the priest or king. Others think of him only as a Savior who forgives sins, but they do not think of him as one who governs their lives. That is the priest without the king. Others think of him mostly as a ruler, but forget that he came to die. The full Jesus is prophet, priest, and king.

The three offices also show what it means to be a Christian. We are united to Christ, and so we share in his offices. Believers are taught by his word, so we listen as prophets who speak the truth. We are priests who offer spiritual sacrifices (1 Peter 2:5, 9). And we are kings who will reign with him, as we learn to rule our own hearts and serve others (Revelation 1:6; 5:10). The offices are not only a way to understand Jesus. They are a way to understand our calling in him.
interpretation:
The three passages you read today are linked by a single idea: God’s final word to his people comes through a person, and that person holds the highest offices in Israel.

Start with Deuteronomy 18. Moses speaks to a people who are afraid of hearing God’s voice directly. At Horeb they said, “Let me not hear again the voice of the LORD my God.” God answered that he would send a prophet like Moses, one who would speak all that God commanded. The people are told, “It is to him you shall listen.” Notice what is required: listening. The whole law of Moses was incomplete, and it pointed forward to a prophet who would complete it. The next verses of the chapter add a stern warning that anyone who does not listen to that prophet will answer for it.

Psalm 110 is the most quoted psalm in the New Testament. In it, David speaks of a figure he calls “my Lord,” someone greater than David himself. This person sits at God’s right hand, which is the place of supreme honor. He is a king, who rules in the midst of his enemies, and he is a priest forever. In Israel, the two roles were kept separate, and kings who tried to act as priests were judged (2 Chronicles 26:16-21). Yet here is one who holds both, and he is established not by descent but by the oath of God. The psalm asks the reader to think about who this could be.

Hebrews 1 gives the answer. The author opens his letter by contrasting the many partial words of the prophets with the one final Word of the Son. Then he describes the Son in three ways: heir of all things and creator of the world (a kingly role), the radiance of God’s glory (a prophetic role, as the one who reveals God), and the one who made purification for sins (a priestly role). Then he says that the Son “sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high,” echoing Psalm 110:1. All three offices come together in a single verse.

Taken together, the passages give a picture of fullness. God spoke in the past in pieces. Now he has spoken in a person. The Son is not just one more messenger. He is the message.
connection: The New Testament repeatedly applies these three offices to Jesus. The crowds said, “This is indeed the Prophet who is to come into the world” (John 6:14). Peter preached that Jesus is the prophet like Moses (Acts 3:22-23), and Stephen did the same (Acts 7:37). Jesus claimed Psalm 110 for himself in front of the Sanhedrin (Mark 14:62). Hebrews 4:14-5:10 and 7:1-28 expound his priesthood. Revelation 19:16 calls him “King of kings and Lord of lords.”
application:
Listen to Jesus as your prophet. Choose a passage in the Gospels today and ask what he is saying to you.

Draw near to him as your priest. Bring a specific need or sin to him in prayer, trusting that he intercedes for you.

Submit to him as your king. Ask whether there is any area of your life that you have not yet put under his rule.
prayerPrompts: Thank Jesus as your prophet, priest, and king, and tell him which of these you most need today.
Ask him to speak, and listen.
Ask him to rule you and help you obey.
